articles.title: El-Sisi urges faster African trade integration, more funding for post-conflict reconstruction - Foreign Affairs - Egypt - Ahram Online
articles.summary: El-Sisi urges faster African trade integration, more funding for post-conflict reconstruction - Foreign Affairs - Egypt  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi called on Sunday for faster African economic integration, full implementation of the continental free trade area, and greater reconstruction funding, closing an African Union meeting in New Alamein.
Addressing the closing session of the eighth AU Mid-Year Coordination Meeting, El-Sisi said continental integration had become “a strategic choice and an urgent necessity” to overcome Africa’s challenges.
The discussions reflected both progress towards integration and the scale of the obstacles requiring coordinated action, he said, according to Presidential Spokesman Mohamed El-Shennawy.
El-Sisi said the meeting’s final declaration provided “a clear roadmap” for advancing regional and continental integration. He urged full implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), alongside stronger supply chains and logistics corridors and the development and interconnection of transport and energy networks.
The call followed his opening address earlier on Sunday, which also stressed deeper African integration.
The president highlighted the urgent need for sustainable, innovative financing for development programmes and projects, in cooperation with African financial institutions.
Financing has also featured in forum discussions, with proposals to mobilize African capital for investment within the continent.
El-Sisi stressed the links between sustainable development, economic growth, and peace and security. He called for stronger conflict-prevention efforts, an improved early-warning mechanism, and greater support for reconstruction and development.
He also urged a larger budget for the Cairo-based AU Center for Post-Conflict Reconstruction and Development to help it operate more effectively, and a stronger role for the centre in continental recovery efforts.
Egypt has previously called for stronger conflict-prevention mechanisms and greater support for the centre.
Turning to private-sector cooperation, El-Sisi welcomed African leaders’ participation in Saturday’s opening of the inaugural Alamein-Africa Business Forum.
He said an official luncheon with leading African investors on Sunday would give leaders a chance to hear business views on advancing economic and trade integration and making better use of Africa’s human and natural resources and investment opportunities.
The gathering would also allow leaders to discuss investors’ proposals for legislative and administrative frameworks that attract and encourage investment, he added.
Separately, NEPAD’s founding states adopted a declaration on Saturday calling for stronger AUDA-NEPAD funding and setting development and investment priorities.
El-Sisi thanked Burundi’s President and AU Chairperson Evariste Ndayishimiye for leading the union this year and chairing the meeting. He also praised AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf and the heads of regional economic communities and regional mechanisms for their contributions to integration.
“I reaffirm Egypt’s full commitment to joint action and cooperation with our fellow African countries to achieve a safe, stable and prosperous Africa,” he concluded.
New Alamein hosted three African gatherings from 2 to 4 October: the AU coordination meeting, the NEPAD founders’ summit and the inaugural business forum.
The Alamein-Africa Business Forum aims to connect African leaders with businesses and financial institutions to turn continental development priorities into investment partnerships and projects.
The coordination meeting examined progress towards economic integration, AU institutional reform and implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area, alongside the union’s 2026 focus on sustainable water availability and safe sanitation.
The African Free Trade Agreement (AfCFTA) entered into force in 2019, during Egypt’s AU chairmanship. It is central to efforts to deepen economic integration under Agenda 2063, the union’s long-term development framework.

articles.title: Absa’s Sitoyo Lopokoiyit points to Tanzania’s mobile money market as Africa’s innovation outlier - TechTrendsKE
articles.summary: Absa’s Sitoyo Lopokoiyit points to Tanzania’s mobile money market as Africa’s innovation outlier  TechTrendsKE
articles.full_text:
Tanzania’s mobile money market has drawn an unusually strong endorsement from Sitoyo Lopokoiyit, Absa’s chief executive for personal and private banking, who describes the country as the world’s most innovative mobile money market.
Speaking to The Citizen Digital, Lopokoiyit pointed to Tanzania’s large population, economic growth and fintech activity, but his comments went beyond the size of the opportunity. He also highlighted a problem that continues to complicate African commerce: moving money between African countries can cost more than moving money outside the continent.
For an executive who previously led M-Pesa Africa, the assessment carries useful context. Lopokoiyit spent much of his career around one of Africa’s most successful mobile-money platforms, and he now sits inside a banking group looking for ways to deepen its digital financial services across multiple markets. His view of Tanzania therefore offers a window into how Absa sees the relationship between mobile money, fintech and conventional banking.
Tanzania’s mobile money market stands out to Sitoyo Lopokoiyit
Lopokoiyit describes Tanzania as a priority market for Absa, citing GDP growth of about 6.3%, inflation of roughly 4.2% to 4.3%, a population of about 70 million and an economy anchored by sectors such as agriculture and mining. Those figures were presented during the interview and refer to the conditions Lopokoiyit was using to explain Absa’s interest in the country.
The mobile-money argument is more distinctive. Kenya has long been associated with M-Pesa and the development of mobile financial services, a point Lopokoiyit acknowledged during the interview. His assessment is that Tanzania has taken mobile-money innovation further than any other market in the world.
That is Lopokoiyit’s characterization rather than an independently measured global ranking, but his background gives the observation particular weight. Before joining Absa, he led M-Pesa Africa across multiple African markets. TechTrendsKE reported in February that the platform had expanded to eight countries, more than 60 million customers and over five million businesses during his tenure.
His experience also puts Tanzania in a wider regional frame. A mobile-money market can be large because it has millions of registered users, but the more important measure for financial institutions is what those users can actually do through the system: receive money, pay merchants, access credit, save, invest, transact with businesses and connect to international services.
Tanzania is already showing some of that breadth. TechTrendsKE reported in May that Vodacom M-Pesa Tanzania had integrated PayPal, allowing eligible users to move money between PayPal accounts and M-Pesa wallets through the M-Pesa Super App. That places a Tanzanian mobile wallet inside a wider digital payments ecosystem rather than leaving it as a domestic transfer tool.
Why Tanzania matters to Absa
Absa’s interest also needs to be understood against the bank’s broader effort to combine conventional banking capabilities with digital financial behaviour.
When Absa appointed Lopokoiyit to lead personal and private banking across Africa, the move brought a mobile-money executive into a business responsible for deposits, lending, investments and other financial products. TechTrendsKE reported at the time that his appointment reflected the growing overlap between telecom-led financial services and traditional banking.
That overlap is visible in Absa’s approach to fintech partnerships. In August, TechTrendsKE reported that the bank was using partnerships to place financial services inside platforms customers already use, with the EasyEquities integration providing one example. Rather than attempting to recreate every service internally, Absa can combine its regulated banking infrastructure and customer base with capabilities developed by fintech companies.
Tanzania gives that strategy an interesting environment in which to operate. The country has a large consumer base, an established mobile-money culture and a growing ecosystem of payment service providers. It also sits within the East African commercial network, where businesses and individuals routinely deal across national borders.
That combination matters because mobile money has changed what customers expect from financial services. People who can send money instantly from a phone do not necessarily accept lengthy processes when they need to make a business payment, receive funds from another country or access a financial product.
From M-Pesa to banking
Lopokoiyit’s move from M-Pesa Africa to Absa is therefore more than a change of employer. His previous role exposed him to the mechanics of scaling digital financial services across markets with different regulators, currencies, consumer habits and banking systems.
TechTrendsKE’s reporting on his appointment described the underlying challenge for Absa: a traditional bank has to manage capital, liquidity, credit risk and regulatory requirements while competing for customers whose everyday financial behaviour is increasingly shaped by mobile platforms.
That helps explain his emphasis on solving problems rather than becoming absorbed by technology itself. In the Tanzania interview, Lopokoiyit argues that financial institutions and technology companies can become fascinated by the tools they are building while losing sight of the problem those tools should solve.
For fintech, that problem can be simple in theory and difficult in practice: make payments cheaper, make settlement predictable, help businesses reach customers in other markets and make financial services accessible without adding unnecessary friction.
Absa’s own digital strategy reflects part of that thinking. In September, Absa Bank Kenya launched Absa Next, a platform combining banking, savings, investments, loans and other services in one digital environment. The platform was built in Kenya and is intended to provide a model for digital banking across the wider Absa Group. Lopokoiyit said Kenya had demonstrated an ability to develop innovations that address real customer problems and influence financial services across Africa.
The Tanzania opportunity fits that philosophy from another direction. The question is whether Absa can take lessons from a market where mobile money has developed in distinctive ways and translate them into banking products, partnerships and payment services that work across its wider African footprint.
The cross-border payments problem
This is where Lopokoiyit’s comments become more significant than the headline about Tanzania’s mobile-money innovation.
He points to an African payments paradox: people can move between countries more freely through regional integration arrangements, yet moving money between those same countries remains expensive and complicated. He argues that the cost of moving money within Africa can exceed the cost of moving it outside the continent.
The problem involves more than technology. Different currencies, regulatory regimes, payment systems, settlement arrangements and foreign-exchange processes all sit between the sender and recipient. A payment can be technically digital while still carrying costs and delays that make cross-border commerce difficult.
That creates space for banks, fintechs and payment networks to compete over the infrastructure underneath the customer experience.
Absa and DHL are already pursuing one piece of this through GoTrade. In September, TechTrendsKE reported that the two companies had agreed to expand the programme across Sub-Saharan Africa, with Tanzania and Mozambique next in line after Uganda. The programme combines trade training, logistics support and financial services to help SMEs reach international markets.
The connection with Lopokoiyit’s comments is direct. He identifies access to markets and access to capital as recurring barriers for innovators, while GoTrade addresses both the commercial and financial obstacles that can prevent smaller businesses from trading across borders.
Absa’s wider African strategy
Absa’s recent moves also show why Tanzania cannot be viewed separately from the bank’s wider African strategy.
The group has been building digital products, working with fintechs and looking for ways to use existing customer behaviour rather than forcing consumers into entirely new financial routines. The appointment of a former M-Pesa Africa chief executive to lead personal and private banking sits squarely within that approach.
The bank’s interest in Kenya provides another example. Absa Group has committed additional capital to its Kenyan subsidiary, while Absa Next is being positioned as a digital model that could have applications elsewhere in the group. TechTrendsKE reported that the group views Kenya’s digital finance ecosystem as a source of innovations that can influence its wider operations.
Tanzania presents a different set of strengths. Its population provides scale, its economy has a substantial agricultural and mining base, and its mobile-money ecosystem gives financial institutions a large pool of established digital behaviour to build around.
That makes the country relevant to Absa’s search for financial services that sit closer to everyday transactions. It also explains why Lopokoiyit places so much emphasis on the problem being solved rather than the technology being deployed.
What Tanzania offers Absa
The most revealing line in the interview may ultimately be Lopokoiyit’s statement that Absa has to “play differently” from other banks.
His comments suggest that difference will have to involve more than putting traditional banking products on a mobile interface. articles.title: El-Sisi urges rapid African transition from raw material exports to building value chains - Egypt Today
articles.summary: El-Sisi urges rapid African transition from raw material exports to building value chains  Egypt Today
articles.full_text:
President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi speaks during the opening session of the 8th African Union Mid-Year Coordination Meeting of the African Union in New Alamein, 4 Oct. 2026. Presidency
CAIRO – 4 October 2026: President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi called on African countries to move quickly from merely exporting raw materials to building value-added chains.
El-Sisi called for working resolutely to localize industries within the continent as he hosted a luncheon on Sunday honoring African heads of state and delegations attending the 8th African Union Mid-Year Coordination Meeting.
The luncheon was also attended by leaders of financing institutions and business representatives who took part in the Alamein Africa Business Forum, the Presidency said.
El-Sisi said the gathering comes at a time of growing and interconnected challenges facing the world, particularly Africa.
He stressed the need for unprecedented African cooperation among countries and organizations, saying the continent’s strength lies in its unity and the integration of its economies.
Int’l Companies’ Role in Africa’s Mega Projects
Addressing international companies attending the luncheon alongside African business leaders, El-Sisi said Africa is no longer merely a consumer market but an emerging manufacturing and technology partner, particularly given its young, educated and ambitious population.
He called on companies to step up efforts to transfer technology and localize industries in African markets.
El-Sisi also urged global companies contribute to major projects across the continent, particularly infrastructure projects, development and energy corridors, renewable energy and other strategic ventures.
From Raw Materials Exportation to Value Chains
El-Sisi said African countries must move quickly from simply exporting raw materials to building value-added chains and working to localize industries within the continent.
Such efforts, he said, would help build a resilient African market capable of withstanding crises and shocks, while serving the interests of African peoples and future generations.
Accelerating AfCFTA Execution
The president also called for accelerating the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), noting that Egypt had played a leading role in advancing the conclusion and entry into force of the agreement.
He urged African countries to work together to remove customs and non-customs barriers and facilitate the movement of goods, services and capital across the continent.
El-Sisi also stressed that economic growth cannot be achieved without a fair global financial system.
Bearing Burdens of Climate Crisis
He said African countries are bearing significant burdens from a climate crisis they did not cause, while also facing unfavorable financing conditions and unprecedented increases in borrowing and debt-servicing costs.
Against this backdrop, he renewed his call for reforming the international financing architecture, providing innovative and affordable financing mechanisms, and granting exemptions related to carbon taxes.

articles.title: LTIF 2026: Where founders meet Ghana’s next growth opportunity - TechCabal
articles.summary: LTIF 2026: Where founders meet Ghana’s next growth opportunity  TechCabal
articles.full_text:
As early-stage capital thins, African founders need more than another funding round to grow. At LTIF 2026 in Accra, the Nigeria-Ghana corridor offers a practical place to find customers, partners, and capital.
African startups raised $1.44 billion in the first half of 2026, level with the same period last year. They did it in 146 disclosed rounds, down from 252. The number of startups raising between $100,000 and $1 million fell 44%, and debt supplied about $614 million of the total.
Capital is concentrating in companies big enough to borrow. For a seed-stage founder, the next round is harder to secure and cannot be the only growth plan. The alternative is revenue from a second market.
Two changes are making Ghana the most logical expansion market for Nigerian founders.
First, payments. On February 3, Onafriq, the cross-border payment fintech, and the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) launched a six-month pilot of what they called the continent’s first wallet-based outbound payment corridor from Nigeria. It settles instantly in local currencies between Nigeria and Ghana, targeting a large trade gap.
Nigeria sold Ghana $139 million of goods in 2024, about 0.2% of its $63.6 billion in exports. Ghana sold Nigeria $52.8 million. Much of West African trade goes unrecorded because banking it is difficult. A founder who fixes settlements is selling into demand the official figures miss.
The second opportunity is regulation. Ghana’s Investment Promotion Authority Act, effective July 15, scrapped the $200,000 and $500,000 minimum-capital rules for joint ventures and wholly foreign-owned companies in most non-trading sectors. A software or services startup can now register a Ghanaian subsidiary without that floor. Traders still need $500,000 in cash, halved from $1 million.
Reserved sectors remain, and the regulator has said the change is not unrestricted liberalisation. The friction is real: Ghanaian and Nigerian traders’ associations have long disputed capital rules and reserved sectors in Ghana’s retail markets.
Capital is already crossing. Ghana joined Morocco and Tanzania in having at least ten startups raise $100,000 or more in the half, yet ranked 11th by total capital raised. Many fundable companies and little money means partners, acquisition targets and co-investors for Nigerian founders.
For Ghanaian founders, Nigeria is the deepest pool on the continent: 40 startups raised $100,000 or more, and $214 million in equity, the most in Africa. Investors have noticed the corridor. Aruwa Capital invested $2 million into Sika Financial, a Ghanaian-founded fintech, to build cross-border settlement rails between the two countries.
The wider market is growing, too. Afreximbank said intra-African trade rose 5.5% to about $213.8 billion in 2025. Yet, that is still only about 16% of the continent’s total trade, which is the headroom.
The opportunity is opening up, but knowing that Ghana is easier to enter is not the same as knowing how to enter it.
A payments company still needs separate licences from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) and the Bank of Ghana (BoG). A founder setting up locally needs to understand which rules apply, who can settle transactions, which partners can move money, and where the first customers are likely to come from.
That is where the Loveworld Trade & Investment Forum (LTIF) comes in. On October 6–7, 2026, Loveworld will bring founders, investors, policymakers, and business leaders together at the Ohene Konadu Auditorium, UPSA, in Accra, Ghana, to work through the practical questions around production, trade, investment readiness, policy access, and pitching.
The forum is free to attend, but registration is mandatory. Its first edition drew over 1,500 business leaders, investors, and entrepreneurs together in Lagos, Nigeria, in 2025.
For a founder considering Ghana, the timing is unusually useful. A new investment law has lowered one barrier to entry, a new payment corridor is being tested, and LTIF puts the people who can help founders navigate both in the same room.

articles.title: President Ramaphosa participates in AU Mid-Year Coordination Meeting in Egypt - South African Government News Agency
articles.summary: President Ramaphosa participates in AU Mid-Year Coordination Meeting in Egypt  South African Government News Agency
articles.full_text:
El-Alamein, Egypt- President Cyril Ramaphosa on Sunday participated in the plenary of the 8th African Union (AU) Mid-Year Coordination Meeting in his capacity as Chairperson of the Southern African Development Community (SADC).
Held in El-Alamein, the Arab Republic of Egypt, the meeting brought together African leaders to deliberate on key continental priorities, including strengthening regional integration, advancing the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), accelerating infrastructure development and addressing peace and security challenges across the continent.
Progress in implementing the division of labour between the African Union, Regional Economic Communities and Member States, alongside efforts to strengthen peace, security and economic cooperation across the continent, were the issues the meeting would discuss, the Presidency said in a post on social media platform X.
READ | President arrives in Egypt for AU meeting 
In a statement, Chairperson of the AU Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf,  said the meeting remains a critical platform for strengthening cooperation between the AU, Regional Economic Communities (RECs) and Regional Mechanisms (RMs)for harmonising efforts towards the implementation of Africa’s continental integration agenda.
Against a complex and rapidly changing global geopolitical environment, the Chairperson stressed the need for Africa to deepen its collective reflection and strengthen its capacity to respond to the challenges affecting peace, security, stability & socio-economic development across the continent.
He further emphasised that, while important progress has been made, institutional operational obstacles continue to constrain regional and continental integration.
“The second decade of Agenda 2063 requires renewed political commitment, stronger coordination & effective implementation of the continental frameworks & instruments already adopted, and a clearer division of labour between the Union, RECs and RMs is essential. 
"Such a division must be based on solidarity, complementarity and comparative advantage, while avoiding duplication and ensuring that collective efforts are directed towards tangible results for African citizens,” said the AU.
The Chairperson reaffirmed the commitment of the AU Commission to working with Member States, RECs & RMs to strengthen peace & stability across the continent.
Youssouf also highlighted the importance of strengthening Africa’s financial architecture and mobilising predictable, sustainable and sufficient resources for the implementation of Agenda 2063.
In his remarks, the President of Egypt, Abdel Fattah El Sisi, welcomed African leaders & delegations to Egypt & stressed the importance of strengthening coordination between the AU, RECs & RMs.
“President El Sisi emphasised that coordination must serve a practical purpose: moving Africa from fragmented efforts towards greater integration, & from shared aspirations towards concrete, implementable projects that deliver tangible benefits to African peoples,” said the African Union.
Bilateral meetings
Meanwhile, on the margins of the AU Mid-Year Coordination Meeting, President Ramaphosa held a bilateral meeting with Chairperson Youssouf.
The engagement provided an opportunity for the two leaders to discuss issues of mutual interest and strengthening cooperation in support of Africa’s integration agenda.
The President also held a bilateral meeting with President El-Sisi to discuss issues of mutual interest and strengthen relations between South Africa and Egypt.
The meeting provided an opportunity for the two leaders to reaffirm the importance of bilateral cooperation and explore areas of shared interest within the broader context of African development and regional collaboration. -SAnews.gov.za

articles.title: STAVROS NICOLAOU | How to fully exploit the Brics opportunity - TimesLIVE
articles.summary: STAVROS NICOLAOU | How to fully exploit the Brics opportunity  TimesLIVE
articles.full_text:
Story audio is generated using AI
South African business is entering a more ambitious phase of engagement with Brics, one defined by deal-making, trade facilitation, investment mobilisation and measurable commercial outcomes. More than a decade after establishing the Brics Business Council, the years of building relationships between South African business and some of the world’s largest and fastest-growing economies are beginning to bear fruit.
South Africa’s participation in Brics has created important relationships that should form part of a broader strategy to diversify our economic partnerships. We should not have to choose between markets or regions. We should ask how major economies can expand the range of opportunities available to South African businesses and strengthen our position within global value chains.
The opportunity becomes clearer when we consider the composition of our trade. Our mineral and agricultural resources remain important assets. The opportunity is to use those strengths as a foundation for greater beneficiation, manufacturing, advanced services, innovation and technology-intensive production.
South Africa already has capabilities across automotive manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, agriculture and agro-processing, machinery, financial services, renewable energy, digital services and critical minerals. The task is to connect these capabilities to international markets and investment partnerships while creating the conditions for South African companies to participate further up global value chains.
Our Brics engagement can create opportunities to move beyond traditional buyer-seller arrangements to co-investment, joint ventures, technology partnerships, manufacturing, research and greater integration into value chains.
Attracting investment and identifying export opportunities is only part of the equation. We also need an enabling environment so that South African companies, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs), can participate in these markets.
For an SME, the difference between a market that exists in principle and one that can be accessed commercially can come down to certification requirements, sanitary and phytosanitary standards, customs processes, regulatory uncertainty, access to trade finance, procurement opportunities and the ability to make and receive cross-border payments. These are not peripheral issues. They can determine whether a business enters a market, integrates into a supply chain, or competes for a commercial opportunity.
We should position South Africa not only as a destination for Brics investment but as a platform from which international companies can build partnerships, establish production and access opportunities across Africa
This is where business matchmaking, procurement linkages, supply chain integration and trade finance become important. For Brics engagement to have a wider economic impact, we need practical pathways that enable smaller South African companies to find partners, secure contracts, enter supply chains and expand into other member markets.
The same applies to technology and innovation. Brics co-operation can support partnerships in areas such as AI, digital services, fintech, green hydrogen, pharmaceuticals and critical minerals. The opportunity is not simply to increase trade in these sectors but to develop partnerships that strengthen research, technology transfer, joint manufacturing and advanced capabilities in South Africa.
The Brics Business Council’s evolution to deal-making and trade facilitation is therefore significant. Its objective should be to connect the institutional relationships and policy dialogue built over more than a decade to specific commercial outcomes, whether through investment partnerships, new export markets, technology transfer, procurement opportunities or more integrated supply chains.
The targets emerging from the 2026 Brics Business Forum provide a useful framework for this shift, including the call to identify and address the 10 most significant trade barriers, setting a target to support 100 Brics start-ups each year to expand into other member markets and facilitating 1,000 new cross-border business partnerships.
For South African business the value of these targets will be determined by what they unlock. This is equally important when considering South Africa’s position as a gateway to Africa. The African Continental Free Trade Area provides an opportunity to connect South African production and services to a much larger continental market. We should therefore position South Africa not only as a destination for Brics investment but as a platform from which international companies can build partnerships, establish production and access opportunities across Africa.
That means attracting partners to South Africa to invest alongside local businesses, develop joint ventures, transfer technology and build capabilities that serve both domestic and continental markets. It also means ensuring that market access created through international engagement translates into opportunities for South African producers and service providers.
South Africa’s Brics presidency in 2028 provides an opportunity to shape an agenda around priorities that reflect our economic circumstances and our position within Africa and the wider Global South. That agenda should not be developed only when the presidency arrives. The work must begin now.
- Nicolaou is a member of the South African Brics Business Council

articles.title: SA launches Joint Business Council with Egypt - South African Government News Agency
articles.summary: SA launches Joint Business Council with Egypt  South African Government News Agency
articles.full_text:
South Africa on Friday elevated its trade and economic relations with Egypt by launching the Joint South Africa - Egypt Business Council (JBC) on the margins of the Alamein- Africa Business Forum.
In a statement, the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (dtic) said Egypt is South Africa’s strategic partner and largest export market in North Africa.
“It has by far the largest population in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, over 102 million, a GDP [gross domestic product] of $362 billion, and is one of Africa’s most diversified, large, and dynamic economies. There are solid opportunities for South African companies in the medium-to-long term and a platform for commercial activities in the Middle East and the Horn of Africa,” said the dtic.
Bilateral trade between South Africa and Egypt has increased.
“According to data received [from] Statistics South Africa, direct bilateral trade increased by 26% from R3.4 billion in 2024 to R4.3 billion in 2025. Secondly, South Africa’s exports to Egypt grew by 21% from R1.3 billion in 2024 to R1.6 billion in 2025. Based on direct data, South Africa had a trade deficit with Egypt from 2021 to 2025.
“These are positive results, making South Africa Egypt’s 46th export destination and 58th source of imports from the rest of the world in 2025,” the department said.
Key initiatives of the JBC include:
-    A launch of a Mining and  Minerals Partnership, Automotive and New-Energy Mobility Partnership.
-    An Agriculture and Agro-processing Corridor, an Engineering and Infrastructure Partnership.
-    A Renewable Energy and Green Industrial Platform. 
-    An Africa Joint-Venture Investment Fund, as a private-sector investment vehicle targeting companies and projects capable of expanding beyond the two domestic markets.
Meanwhile, dtic Minister Parks Tau participated in the Africa Automotive Investment Forum, held on the margins of the inaugural Alamein Africa Forum in Egypt, under the theme “Unlocking Africa’s Automotive Industry Potential under the AfCFTA.”
READ | Call for stronger partnerships to drive automotive investment, job creation
The Forum was hosted by Dr Mohamed Farid Saleh, the Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade, Government of Egypt, in collaboration with Afreximbank and the African Association of Automotive Manufacturers (AAAM). Participants at the Forum observed the signing and launch of the Joint Business Council between South Africa and Egypt.
“The outcome of this relationship results in deepening bilateral trade and investment by creating practical commercial partnerships between South African and Egyptian companies, while using both countries as gateways into Southern, North and wider African markets,” the department explained.
For South Africa, the Forum provided an opportunity to position the country as a key manufacturing and investment anchor within an emerging continental automotive value chain, while strengthening linkages between South African automotive producers, African markets, component manufacturers, logistics networks and sources of capital.
The Forum brought together policymakers, governments, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), component manufacturers, suppliers, investors, financiers, logistics providers and development partners to identify bankable investment opportunities, strengthen regional automotive production capabilities and advance the development of integrated continental supply chains. -SAnews.gov.za

articles.title: China-Thailand joint port expansion project bolsters Maritime Silk Road connectivity - bastillepost.com
articles.summary: China-Thailand joint port expansion project bolsters Maritime Silk Road connectivity  bastillepost.com
articles.full_text:
Chinese firms are partnering with Thai builders on a new round of port expansion project, the Phase-III expansion work of Laem Chabang Port.
Improved port infrastructure and logistics networks are expected to open up new opportunities for the port to connect with China and global markets and boost Thailand's industrial development, making it an important connectivity node in the country for the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road.
Located in Chonburi Province in eastern Thailand, around 130 km from Bangkok, Laem Chabang Port sits adjacent to the Eastern Economic Corridor, Thailand's manufacturing hub. Every day, huge volumes of containers, automobiles, machinery equipment and agricultural products are shipped from the port to destinations across the globe.
Dozens of kilometers around the port lie multiple large industrial parks, home to clustered manufacturers of automobiles, electronics and machinery.
In the ongoing new round of expansion, Chinese contractors are undertaking Phase-III infrastructure works, including 29 port roads, 16 bridges, a 500‑meter-long coastal berth and supporting container yards.
"Thai‑Chinese cooperation on this construction project is highly important. It helps push forward smooth project delivery and ensures the highest quality and safety standards. Aligned with the Maritime Silk Road initiative, it facilitates Thailand’s trade with the rest of the world. Laem Chabang Port will become a vital hub driving Thailand's trade toward global markets," said Anuson, Thai-side manager for the Chinese-run infrastructure projects.
Upon completion of Phase-III, the port's annual container handling capacity will rise from the current 11 million TEUs to about 18 million TEUs, further strengthening Thailand's logistics capacity linking regional and global markets.
The project has also nurtured a large pool of local engineers and technical personnel.
Pattarapong, a Thai engineer, said the role has brought her steady employment while exposing her to new construction techniques and management practices, building up her hands-on experience in large-scale port construction.
"Local workers account for roughly 70 percent of staff on the ongoing construction site. The Chinese enterprise attaches great importance to creating local jobs and keeps recruiting people from surrounding communities. I am delighted and honored to take part in this project since it is also part of the Maritime Silk Road development," said Pattarapong.
Earlier this year, a new shipping route linking Yantian Port in south China's Shenzhen City, Laem Chabang Port, and Cambodia's Sihanoukville Port was officially launched. It is expected to deepen ties between Thailand and China's Guangdong‑Hong Kong‑Macao Greater Bay Area, and open a fresh cargo import‑export corridor for businesses.
On land, Thailand is pressing ahead with the construction of a railway collection‑and‑distribution system for the port, with plans to boost freight rail links between Laem Chabang Port and northeastern Thailand.
Via maritime shipping lines and overland transport links, Laem Chabang Port connects with Thailand's industrial heartland. As regional transport networks keep improving, the port will further leverage its strengths in combined sea‑and‑land transport.
Over the past 13 years, projects such as this one under the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road have delivered fresh support for connectivity between China and Southeast Asian countries.
The 21st Century Maritime Silk Road is the sea route part of the Belt and Road Initiative proposed by China.

The global mining dispersants market represents a specialized segment of the mining chemicals industry, encompassing anionic, cationic, nonionic, and polymeric dispersant formulations, surfactant blends, and additives designed to enhance mineral processing efficiency. These chemicals play a critical role in reducing particle agglomeration, improving slurry transport, optimizing ore flotation, and supporting tailings management and dewatering. Demand is fundamentally tied to the operational performance of mineral extraction and processing, with value propositions centered on reducing energy consumption, increasing mineral recovery rates, and lowering water usage.

This growth is underpinned by steady expansion in global mineral production, particularly for critical minerals essential to the energy transition, and by the increasing adoption of dispersants to improve operational efficiency in mining processes. The market is expected to benefit from rising investments in tailings management and water conservation, as mining companies face stricter environmental regulations and community pressure to reduce water usage and improve dam safety.
Additionally, the depletion of high-grade ore bodies is forcing operators to process more complex and finer-grained ores, which increases the demand for specialized dispersants to maintain recovery rates and throughput. Raw material availability, particularly for specialty surfactants and polymers, remains a potential bottleneck, but ongoing capacity expansions are expected to alleviate some pressure. Overall, the market is poised for moderate but consistent growth, with opportunities in emerging mining regions and in the development of environmentally friendly dispersant formulations.
Coal processing remains a significant application for mining dispersants, particularly in coal preparation plants where dispersants are used to improve the efficiency of fine coal separation and dewatering. In this segment, dispersants help reduce the moisture content of clean coal, enhance the performance of froth flotation, and facilitate the handling of coal slurries. However, the global shift away from coal as an energy source, driven by climate policies and the growth of renewable energy, is expected to temper demand growth in this sector.
Through 2035, coal processing dispersant demand will likely decline in Europe and North America, but remain stable or grow modestly in Asia-Pacific, where coal continues to play a key role in power generation and industrial processes. The trend toward cleaner coal technologies may also create opportunities for more efficient dispersant formulations that reduce water usage and improve fine coal recovery. Dangote Group has urged Nigeria to strengthen domestic production, reduce import dependence and expand exports to build economic resilience and competitiveness.
The Regional Director of Dangote Group, Hajia Fatima Wali-Abdurrahman, made the call on Friday at the group’s special day at the 21st Abuja International Trade Fair.
Wali-Abdurrahman, who was represented by the Group General Manager, Mr Abdullahi Dan-Musa, stressed that economic resilience depended on expanding productive capacity and strengthening local supply chains.

She called for an investment environment that encouraged industrial growth, job creation, exports and sustainable economic development.
Wali-Abdurrahman noted that businesses were contending with inflationary pressures, exchange-rate adjustments, evolving tax policies and technological disruptions.
She added that changing international trade patterns were also creating new challenges for businesses operating in Nigeria.
According to her, economic resilience went beyond withstanding difficulties to include adapting, innovating and continuing to invest in the future.
“Dangote Group remains committed to building productive capacity across Nigeria and Africa through investments that create jobs and strengthen local supply chains,” Wali-Abdurrahman said.
She explained that the group’s investments covered cement, sugar, salt, seasoning, packaging, fertiliser, petrochemicals and petroleum refining, among other sectors.
Wali-Abdurrahman said Dangote Cement had helped transform Nigeria from a major cement-importing market into a significant producer and exporter.
“The company’s operations support employment while sustaining suppliers, distributors, contractors, transporters, retailers and other businesses across the value chain,” she noted.
She disclosed that the group had extended its Pan-African industrial vision to the energy sector, with construction beginning on its refinery and petrochemicals project in Lamu, Kenya.
Wali-Abdurrahman explained that local manufacturing generated wider economic benefits by creating contracts, expanding distribution networks and supporting transportation.
She added that manufacturing also helped develop technical skills among young Nigerians while strengthening domestic supply chains.
Wali-Abdurrahman stressed that taxation remained essential for funding infrastructure, education, healthcare, security and other public services that support economic activity.
She, however, called for a predictable, transparent and efficient tax environment that would encourage compliance without discouraging investment and innovation.
Wali-Abdurrahman disclosed that Dangote Petroleum Refinery currently had a refining capacity of 700,000 barrels per day, with expansion to 1.4 million barrels planned.
She explained that the refinery would support energy security, reduce dependence on imported refined products and conserve foreign exchange.
The Dangote Group Regional Director added that the facility would also help develop local technical expertise and strengthen Nigeria’s industrial capacity.
Wali-Abdurrahman said the group’s Vision 2030 was aimed at transforming Dangote Industries Ltd. into a $100 billion enterprise through industrial expansion and cross-border investments across Africa.
Speaking at the event, the First Deputy President of the Abuja Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI), Prof. Adesoji Adesugba, commended Dangote Group for its longstanding partnership with the chamber.
Adesugba, who represented the ACCI President, Chief Emeka Obegolu, said the trade fair had evolved beyond an exhibition platform into an important economic marketplace.
He explained that the fair brought together businesses, investors, government institutions, diplomatic missions, entrepreneurs and consumers to create commercial relationships.
The ACCI official noted that the platform also stimulated economic activity and provided opportunities for businesses to gain visibility and access customers.
He said the fair enabled participants to identify investment opportunities and strengthen value chains through commercial relationships.
Adesugba described the partnership between Dangote and ACCI as an example of the role of responsible corporate participation in sustaining platforms that promote commerce and enterprise.
He noted that Dangote’s investments in cement, fertiliser, agriculture, refining and petrochemicals demonstrated the importance of domestic productive capacity.
The ACCI First Deputy President added that the investments supported employment creation and reduced Nigeria’s dependence on imports.
Adesugba said ACCI recognised Dangote not only as an exhibitor and sponsor, but also as a strategic partner whose investments supported Nigerian businesses, trade, investment and sustainable economic development.

The Vietnam-South Africa Economic, Trade, and Investment Cooperation Prospects Forum, held in Cape Town (Republic of South Africa) on October 2, 2026, opened a space for practical exchanges between management agencies, trade promotion organizations, and business communities of the two countries, aiming to concretize cooperation potential within the framework of the Strategic Partnership.
According to information from the Trade Promotion Agency, on October 2, 2026, a forum on prospects for economic, trade, and investment cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa took place in Cape Town, Republic of South Africa . The forum was attended by leaders of the Vietnamese National Assembly, representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade , the Vietnamese Embassy in South Africa, the Western Cape Tourism, Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (WESGRO), relevant agencies, and the business communities of both countries.
The forum is one of the important activities within the framework of the official visit of the high-level delegation of the Vietnamese National Assembly to Cape Town, the legislative capital of South Africa.
The forum focused on exchanging views on the business environment, trade and investment opportunities, relevant policies and regulations, and discussing areas with potential for extensive cooperation in the future.
Deepening the Strategic Partnership into an economic one.
In his opening remarks at the Forum, Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien emphasized that over the past 30 years, the friendship and cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa have developed in a substantive and effective manner. The upgrading of relations to a Strategic Partnership in November 2025 opens a new framework for cooperation with a long-term vision and higher demands for quality and effectiveness. Economic, trade, and investment cooperation is identified as one of the important pillars.
According to the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly, bilateral trade turnover is projected to reach approximately US$1.3 billion in 2025; and over US$1.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026, a 45% increase compared to the same period last year. South Africa is currently Vietnam's second largest trading partner and its largest export market in Africa; while Vietnam is South Africa's fifth largest trading partner in the ASEAN region.
However, the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly stated that these results are still not commensurate with the potential and strengths of the two economies, as well as the Strategic Partnership between the two countries.
The two economies complement each other in many ways. South Africa has strengths in resources, industry, services, finance, and its gateway location to the African market; while Vietnam has strengths in manufacturing, processing, agriculture , technology, electronics, telecommunications, international trade, and experience in participating in value chains.
Based on that foundation, the two sides can expand cooperation in high value-added areas such as processing and manufacturing industries, digital transformation , artificial intelligence, green economy, renewable energy, mining and mineral processing, high-tech agriculture, and supporting industries.
In particular, the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly emphasized the need to build a favorable legal environment to transform cooperation potential into concrete projects and capital flows: "Businesses need an investment and business environment where regulations are clear, transparent, stable, and predictable; procedures are simplified; compliance costs are minimized; and legitimate rights and interests are guaranteed."
The Vice Chairman of the National Assembly affirmed that the Vietnamese National Assembly and Government are ready to cooperate with the National Assembly, Government, and relevant agencies of South Africa to create an effective bridge for the business communities of the two countries.
For his part, JP van der Merwe, Deputy Director for Investment at the Western Cape Tourism, Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (WESGRO), South Africa, stated that South Africa is the most industrialized and diversified economy in Africa, with a size of $363 billion, a market of 63 million people, preferential access to African markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), and is home to approximately half of the multinational corporations operating in Africa.
WESGRO recognizes that the Western Cape region of South Africa has significant potential for cooperation with Vietnamese businesses in areas such as renewable energy, green hydrogen, electric vehicles, battery manufacturing, high-tech agriculture, agricultural product processing, logistics, and information technology services. To support investors and importers, the agency has developed the Cape Trade Portal, connecting over 2,100 exporters in the region with buyers worldwide.

The scale of goods trade increased from approximately US$668.5 billion in 2021 to approximately US$930 billion in 2025. Along with this, Vietnam continues to maintain its ability to attract foreign investment, with registered FDI capital reaching approximately US$38.42 billion in 2025 and implemented capital reaching US$27.62 billion.
These results show that Vietnam is not only a consumer market but is increasingly becoming a production and export hub in the region.
For South Africa, this provides a basis for both sides to study complementary cooperation models, ranging from supplying raw materials and inputs, cooperating in deep processing, developing supporting industries, to expanding markets for products in which each country has a competitive advantage.
Director Vu Ba Phu affirmed that the Trade Promotion Department is ready to play a bridging role, supporting businesses of both countries in understanding markets, finding partners, and implementing specific cooperation opportunities.
International trade promotion programs and events such as Vietnam Expo, Vietnam Foodexpo, VIATT, Vietnam Global International Fair, along with business networking and exchange programs, are presented as practical channels for South African businesses to gain deeper access to the Vietnamese market.
“ We hope to invite South African trade promotion agencies, associations, and businesses to participate more deeply in programs in Vietnam, not only as visitors but also to participate in exhibitions, B2B trade, supplier search, investment partner search, and building long-term cooperative relationships, ” said Mr. Vu Ba Phu.
Therefore, the Trade Promotion Department proposed strengthening market information exchange, connecting businesses by industry, building regular cooperation programs between associations and trade promotion organizations, and increasing two-way business delegations to survey markets and seek investment opportunities.
Strengthening cooperation in the energy sector, including coal trade.

According to discussions at the Forum, Vietnam's coal import needs will remain significant in the coming period, while South Africa has strengths in coal mining and exporting, and possesses a large-scale infrastructure system to support exports.

South Africa’s foreign investment landscape strengthens as FDI inflows rise, major infrastructure commitments expand, and opportunities grow across energy, mining, manufacturing, logistics, digital infrastructure and green industries.
South Africa’s investment landscape is showing renewed momentum in 2026 as foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows, large-scale investment commitments and infrastructure spending create new opportunities across energy, mining, manufacturing, logistics and digital infrastructure. The latest data from the South African Reserve Bank show that FDI inflows reached R49.8 billion (about US$3.03 billion) in Q2 2026, more than double the R20.3 billion (about US$1.24 billion) recorded in Q1 2026.
The increase comes as the government steps up efforts to attract domestic and international capital through structural reforms, infrastructure development and sector-specific investment programmes. At the 6th South Africa Investment Conference in March 2026, investment commitments reached R889.8 billion (about US$54.2 billion), involving 81 projects across all nine provinces and 22 source markets.
South Africa is also pursuing a longer-term investment ambition of R3 trillion (about US$182.7 billion) by 2030, while more than R1 trillion (about US$61 billion) is planned for infrastructure investment over the next three years. These developments are positioning infrastructure, energy transition, manufacturing, mining beneficiation, logistics and digital services as important areas for future capital deployment.
Foreign Direct Investment Inflows Surge in Q2 2026
South Africa’s latest foreign investment data indicate stronger capital activity during the second quarter of 2026. The improvement came amid ongoing efforts to strengthen the country’s investment environment and address structural constraints affecting business activity. Government initiatives have focused on electricity, logistics, infrastructure and other network industries, with greater emphasis on private-sector participation and investment partnerships. The 2026 Investment Conference also highlighted reforms aimed at improving infrastructure delivery and creating additional opportunities for domestic and international investors.
However, quarterly FDI movements can be influenced by individual transactions, making it important to interpret short-term changes alongside broader investment trends. The country’s wider international investment position also strengthened during the period, supported by changes in the valuation of foreign assets and liabilities. Together, these developments indicate continued investor engagement with South Africa’s economy and reinforce the importance of reforms, infrastructure development and improved investment conditions in attracting long-term capital.

The European Union and Canada are preparing a new, large-scale partnership, which they plan to announce in late October. According to Politico, the agreements will cover trade, energy, critical resources and technologies, as well as support for Ukraine. However, specific measures to assist Kyiv have not yet been disclosed.
The European Union and Canada are preparing a new package of cooperation agreements. Politico reports this, citing a draft joint statement that was obtained by journalists. The new partnership is set to be announced during the EU-Canada summit in Montreal on October 29–30. The summit itself has already been officially scheduled by the Council of the EU.
According to the publication, the future cooperation will cover several areas at once. These include trade, energy, technology, critical resources, and security. One area of focus will be support for Ukraine. However, it is not yet clear exactly what new measures the EU and Canada might offer Kyiv.
They Want to Invest More in Critical Resources
The EU and Canada plan to pay special attention to critical minerals. These are resources needed for modern industry, energy, the defense sector, and new technologies. Brussels and Ottawa want to accelerate investment in their extraction.
The parties also plan to strengthen supply chains. Specifically, this involves building up strategic resource reserves to reduce dependence on potential disruptions in global markets.
The draft joint statement notes that this should help the countries better respond to price fluctuations and geopolitical risks. “We will align strategies and standards, bring industries together, and focus our ambitions on sectors that will bring the greatest benefits to our peoples,” the draft document states.
Cooperation will cover trade and technology
The EU and Canada also aim to streamline digital trade and remove some barriers to business. The countries plan to cooperate more closely in the areas of technology, energy, and economic security. A separate area of focus is the protection of critical supply chains and access to strategic resources.
This is not an entirely new area for Brussels and Ottawa. The EU and Canada already have a partnership on critical raw materials, as well as agreements on security and defense. In June 2025, the parties separately reaffirmed their support for Ukraine and agreed to deepen cooperation in the field of critical minerals.
In 2026, defense cooperation also expanded. Canada became the first country outside Europe to join the EU’s SAFE mechanism, which facilitates joint defense procurement.
What Ukraine Will Gain
Ukraine is also set to become part of a new partnership between the EU and Canada. According to Politico, the parties plan to strengthen their joint support for Kyiv. At the same time, the draft document does not yet specify exactly what kind of assistance is being discussed.
Therefore, it is currently unknown whether this will involve new financial measures, military aid, joint investments, or other programs. More details are expected to emerge during the summit in Montreal in late October.
The EU and Canada have already officially declared their support for Ukraine. In 2025, the parties reaffirmed their readiness to continue providing political, financial, economic, humanitarian, military, and diplomatic assistance to Ukraine.

articles.title: The Busiest Cargo Ports - WorldAtlas
articles.summary: The Busiest Cargo Ports  WorldAtlas
articles.full_text:
More than half of the cargo moving through America’s 150 busiest water ports passes through the Gulf Coast. In 2023, those 150 ports handled about 2.6 billion short tons, and 52% of that tonnage moved through Gulf ports. The concentration is even sharper at the top: half of all tonnage passed through just 10 ports. As of 2026, the latest nationally consistent federal ranking uses 2023 cargo data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Waterborne Commerce Statistics Center.
Port Houston
No state comes close to Texas at the top of the federal port ranking. Port Houston handled 309.5 million short tons in 2023, making it the busiest U.S. water port by total tonnage. Corpus Christi added another 189.8 million tons that year, while Beaumont moved 87.9 million, illustrating how much Texas cargo is spread among several major Gulf ports.
Houston’s weight comes largely from the petroleum, chemical, and industrial trade surrounding the Houston Ship Channel, although its public terminals also handle containers and steel. The port remains active at enormous scale in 2026: through July, the wider Houston Ship Channel region had already moved 155.6 million short tons of foreign waterborne cargo, while Port Houston’s public terminals handled nearly 3 million TEUs through August.
Port of South Louisiana
The Port of South Louisiana handled 217.5 million short tons under the federal definition in 2023, second only to Houston. Its location along 54 miles of the Mississippi River places more than 40 liquid and dry-bulk terminals within the port district. Grain, petroleum products, chemicals, and other bulk commodities account for much of the traffic.
This port is also a good example of why one source must be used consistently for a national ranking. The Port of South Louisiana reported 248.3 million short tons of total trade for 2025 under its own accounting boundaries, considerably above the 217.5-million-ton federal figure from 2023. Both can be accurate because they measure somewhat different areas and movements.
Port of New York and New Jersey
The Port of New York and New Jersey handled 132.3 million short tons in 2023, making it the highest-ranked port outside the Gulf Coast. Because the federal port spans both states, splitting its tonnage between New York and New Jersey would create an artificial result. It is therefore treated as one interstate entry here.
Unlike Houston and South Louisiana, New York-New Jersey is particularly important for containerized consumer goods. Its facilities include Port Newark, Elizabeth, Port Jersey, and Howland Hook. The Port Authority’s 2025 budget described a system moving roughly 5 million physical containers through its docks each year, while continued capital spending through 2026 is expanding rail and terminal capacity.
Port of Long Beach
California’s highest-tonnage entry is Long Beach, which moved 85.3 million short tons in 2023. That placed it sixth nationally in the federal ranking, ahead of neighboring Los Angeles at 55.4 million tons.
Tonnage does not fully capture the role of the San Pedro Bay ports because so much of their cargo consists of relatively light, high-value containerized goods. Long Beach handled a record 9.9 million TEUs in 2025, compared with its 85.3-million-short-ton federal total in 2023. The difference illustrates why a port can rank differently depending on whether the measurement is total weight or containers.
Port of Virginia
Virginia’s Hampton Roads port complex handled 68.8 million short tons in 2023, ranking ninth among all U.S. ports. Coal is a major reason for the high weight total, while container traffic forms another large part of the port’s business.
In calendar year 2025, Hampton Roads handled 63.4 million short tons of total cargo, including about 34.1 million tons of coal loadings and 3.24 million TEUs. Infrastructure also changed in 2026, when the Port of Virginia completed a $450 million project that deepened its commercial shipping channel to 55 feet.
Port of Mobile
The Port of Mobile handled 52.2 million short tons in 2023, placing Alabama ahead of every remaining state on this list. Its cargo mix includes coal, forest products, steel, containers, and other bulk and breakbulk shipments.
Mobile’s navigation channel reached a depth of 50 feet in October 2025 following a $366 million modernization project. Another $131 million container-berth project announced later that month is designed to raise berth capacity to 1.4 million TEUs annually after completion. Operations continued expanding in 2026, including construction of a new export facility projected to add about 60,000 TEUs of annual capacity.
Port of Baltimore
Baltimore handled 49.9 million short tons in the federal 2023 ranking, placing it 14th nationally and first in Maryland. Its location on Chesapeake Bay combines bulk terminals with container, automobile, and roll-on/roll-off facilities.
The port’s 2025 figures show how quickly cargo volumes recovered following the 2024 Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse and temporary shipping-channel closure. Public and private terminals handled about 50 million tons in 2025, including 1.1 million TEUs, 728,225 automobiles, and 848,628 tons of roll-on/roll-off farm and construction machinery.
Port of Savannah
Only about 638,000 short tons separated Savannah from Baltimore in the 2023 federal ranking. Savannah handled 49.2 million short tons, making it Georgia’s busiest port by tonnage and 15th nationally.
Containers are the more familiar measure of Savannah’s activity. The Georgia Ports Authority reported nearly 5.7 million TEUs in calendar year 2025, the port’s second-highest annual total. Savannah also handled 545,214 containers by rail during 2025 and averaged between 14,000 and 16,000 truck moves on weekdays.
Oil and Big Boxes
The accelerated development of ports in the United States during the 20th century centered around two primary features: mobilizing oil and the invention of the modern container. In the South and West, oil has been king from the start of the 20th century as the primary driver bringing in waves of fortune seekers.
The 2023 federal figures reveal two different versions of a busy American port. By weight, petroleum, coal, grain, ores, and other bulk cargo push Gulf Coast and industrial ports toward the top. Houston alone moved 309.5 million short tons in 2023, almost six times Savannah’s 49.2 million. Container rankings tell a different story. Los Angeles led the country with 5.73 million loaded TEUs in 2023, followed by New York-New Jersey at 5.40 million and Long Beach at 5.09 million. Savannah ranked fourth at 3.77 million loaded TEUs despite sitting only 15th in the tonnage table.

The eighth mid-year coordination meeting of the African Union (AU) and Regional Economic Communities (RECs) convened in Egypt on Sunday.
The event brings together several African heads of state to discuss progress on the AU's 2026 theme regarding assuring sustainable water availability and safe sanitation systems to achieve the goals of Agenda 2063.
The meeting further drilled down on the latest developments in continental efforts to strengthen coordination and integration among Africa's RECs, advance implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and drive forward the AU's institutional development.
In his inaugural remarks, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi said the meeting explores avenues for enhancing existing coordination among the AU, the economic communities and regional mechanisms to help reinforce sustainable development efforts in African nations, navigate from a multiplicity of efforts to integration, and move from shared ambitions to limited, implementable projects and programs that achieve a concrete impact on the lives of African peoples.
El-Sisi underlined Egypt's unyielding position in pushing back against any foreign intervention in the internal affairs of African nations, emphasizing that Egypt calls for respecting nations' sovereignty and territorial integrity as the essence and indispensable principles for the stability of Africa.
Relationships among African nations should be based on mutual respect, neighborly relations, as well as dialogue and consultation rather than unilateral policies or parochial interests, El-Sisi stressed.
He advocated for the full operationalization of AfCFTA, which entered into force in 2019, thereby unlocking prospects for a truly integrated African market that can capitalize on the continent's enormous productive capacity, boost intra-African trade, support industrialization and technology transfer, and create more job opportunities.
Having weighed in during the meeting, President of the Republic of Burundi and AU Chairperson Evariste Ndayishimiye said the meeting aims to unify efforts among African nations and advance continental integration by achieving the objectives of Agenda 2063.
He underscored that managing African resources is of the essence in solidarity and collaboration with African countries, asserting that the success of regional integration hinges on an economic consensus among African nations.
Ndayishimiye further pointed out that the AU is working to achieve stability in Africa to curb ongoing geopolitical tensions in the global political context, as well as address challenges pertaining to the peace architecture that affect regional integration in Africa.

articles.title: AU Mid-Year Coordination Meeting: Decisions, Regional Blocs and Egypt's Priorities - Sada Elbalad English
articles.summary: AU Mid-Year Coordination Meeting: Decisions, Regional Blocs and Egypt's Priorities  Sada Elbalad English
articles.full_text:
NEW ALAMEIN, 4 October 2026: African leaders gathered in Egypt on Sunday for a meeting that rarely makes headlines but shapes how the continent's institutions actually work together.
What is this meeting for?
The Mid-Year Coordination Meeting is not a regular summit. It is usually limited to a few African leaders, and its purpose is to coordinate between the African Union, the regional economic communities and regional mechanisms. In practice, it tackles one question: who does what when the AU and the regional blocs both claim a role, whether on trade, security or financing.
This is the eighth edition. The AU decided to hold it in El Alamein on 4 October 2026, after the original June date was moved.
Why Egypt's role matters
As host, President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi delivered the opening speech on Sunday morning and is due to deliver the closing address. Egypt also arrives with a record on the agenda. Cairo stresses President Sisi's leadership of the AU's post-conflict reconstruction and development agenda, and this year marks the 20th anniversary of the AU's Post-Conflict Reconstruction and Development Policy. A Peace and Security Council subcommittee on reconstruction held its first meeting in February 2026 under Egypt's chairmanship of the Council.
The meeting also follows a busy weekend in Alamein, including the first Alamein Africa Business Forum and a summit of the founding states of the AU Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD). Egypt will host the forum's second edition in 2028
What was said
In his opening address, President Sisi framed coordination as a means rather than a goal: the point, he said, is to move from multiple efforts to integrated ones that produce projects with tangible impact. It is no longer enough to coordinate positions, he argued; capabilities must integrate. That is the "division of labour" question in the President's own terms.
Three of his messages map directly onto the issues to watch. On trade, he called for full activation of the AfCFTA and for value chains built inside Africa. On reconstruction, he said rebuilding states is an integral part of the continent's peace and security system, used Alamein itself, once a battlefield, as the example, and renewed Egypt's support for the AU's reconstruction work, including the Cairo-based centre. On water, the AU's theme for 2026, he welcomed the Africa Water Vision and Policy 2063 and said cooperation on transboundary rivers must rest on international law and the principle of no harm.
He also rejected external interference in African states' internal affairs, and stressed the unity and territorial integrity of states.
The AU Commission's view. Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf went to the heart of the meeting's purpose, saying the success of economic integration rests on a clear division of roles between the AU and the regional economic communities, and on financing. He said the regional communities keep pushing integration forward, but institutional and operational obstacles still hold back continental work, and called for African resources to be directed toward the continent and for more intra-African trade.
The AU chair's view. Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, the AU's current chairperson, asked for a clear division of roles between the AU, the regional communities and member states under the principles of subsidiarity and complementarity, to prevent overlapping mandates. He named Sudan, the Great Lakes region, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Sahel as security concerns, and called for moving from early warning to early action. He also stressed that a free trade area needs production capacity behind it, and that the AU needs predictable financing to implement its decisions.
Eight issues to watch
How to judge the outcome
The meeting is expected to close with a final outcome document.. The useful test is concrete: does it name responsibilities and timelines on these issues, or does it restate principles? We will update this piece with the closing address and the final declaration as they are released.

Burundi’s President, Evariste Ndayishimiye, has called for stronger investment partnerships among African countries to accelerate economic growth, industrialisation and development across the continent.
Ndayishimiye made the call at the inaugural Alamein Africa Forum in Egypt, attended by African heads of state, continental institutions, financial organisations and business leaders.
The Burundian leader stressed the need for Africa to move beyond traditional diplomatic partnerships towards economic, investment and production partnerships that would transform the continent’s abundant resources into productive activities.
He called for stronger implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area, supported by improved trade corridors, integrated border posts, harmonised customs procedures, cross-border payment systems, trade finance, logistics and regional value chains.
Ndayishimiye also proposed an African Investment and Implementation Dashboard to track strategic continental projects, investments, financing, responsibilities, timelines and measurable results.
He stressed that every commitment should lead to a project, every project should secure financing and every investment should produce results that contribute to Africa’s integration and prosperity.
The African Union said the forum brought governments and the private sector together to translate the continent’s development ambitions into well-prepared, financed and implemented projects.
The Union noted that Africa had vast agricultural potential, strategic minerals, abundant energy resources, a youthful population and a continental market anchored by the African Continental Free Trade Area.
It said the continent needed to use its resources to create value, build industries, generate jobs and strengthen its economic resilience.
Also speaking at the forum, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi called for stronger African economic cooperation, continental integration and greater private-sector participation in development.
El-Sisi stressed that African countries had the right to pursue development and benefit from their natural resources while respecting one another’s rights and avoiding actions that could harm other countries.
“Our common interests are greater than our differences,” he said.
The Egyptian President also highlighted the critical role of the African private sector in driving growth and employment, urging stronger connections among African businesses and greater access to information on investment and trade opportunities across neighbouring markets.
The forum provided a platform for African governments, businesses, financial institutions and investors to strengthen partnerships, promote intra-African trade and advance the implementation of the African Union’s Agenda 2063.
Ndayishimiye, however, warned that persistent insecurity remained a major obstacle to development in parts of Africa, disrupting farming, education and government planning.
“Amid insecurity, no farmer goes to the fields anymore. No child goes to school anymore. No institution plans development for its country,” he said.
He expressed concern over continued conflicts in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Sudan, describing the situation as an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe.
The Alamein Africa Forum was established as a platform for strengthening economic cooperation, investment and cross-border partnerships, with the inaugural edition running from October 2 to October 4 in New Alamein City.
