articles.title: China-Africa mining pact a path to shared prosperity - standardmedia.co.ke
articles.summary: China-Africa mining pact a path to shared prosperity  standardmedia.co.ke
articles.full_text:
Africa’s mineral wealth has never been more strategically important. Copper, cobalt, lithium, rare earth elements, graphite and other critical minerals are essential to the global energy transition and technologies shaping the future economy.
                            
For Africa, this presents an extraordinary opportunity. The continent has some of the world’s richest mineral deposits, yet much of it has historically left as raw material, with higher-value processing taking place elsewhere. The challenge now is to ensure Africa captures a greater share of the value created by its resources.
This is where China-Africa mining cooperation deserves serious attention. China has emerged as an important partner in Africa’s mining sector, bringing investment, technology, infrastructure, industrial expertise and experience across the mineral value chain. Its engagement offers African countries an opportunity to move beyond extraction and build stronger industries around their natural resources.
Demand for critical minerals is rising rapidly as countries invest in electric vehicles, batteries, renewable energy, telecommunications and advanced technologies. Africa is home to many of the resources required for this transformation. Connecting those resources with investment and industrial capacity can create a new chapter in Africa’s economic development.
                            
China’s experience is particularly relevant because its own economic transformation has been built around industrialisation, infrastructure and manufacturing. Its mining sector has developed capabilities spanning exploration, extraction, processing, equipment manufacturing and increasingly green and intelligent mining.
For African countries seeking to move up the value chain, that experience provides an important foundation for cooperation.
The strongest mining partnerships go beyond extraction to create jobs, transfer skills, develop infrastructure, support local businesses and retain greater value within African economies. This is an area where China-Africa cooperation offers considerable potential.
Countries such as Zambia, Zimbabwe and the Democratic Republic of Congo possess significant deposits of copper, cobalt and lithium. Expanding processing and refining capacity can create opportunities for manufacturing, skilled employment and technology development.
                            
Infrastructure is equally important. Roads, railways, ports, electricity and water systems are essential to mining, but their value can extend far beyond individual projects. When properly integrated into national development plans, mining-related infrastructure can connect communities to markets, support agriculture and stimulate new businesses.
The Simandou iron ore project in Guinea illustrates the scale of infrastructure that can accompany major mining investment, including a deepwater port and a 626-kilometre railway connecting mining areas to the coast.
Technology presents another major opportunity.
At the 2026 China Mining Conference and Exhibition in Tianjin, Chinese companies showcased green technologies, intelligent equipment and digital mining solutions designed to improve mineral recovery, reduce energy consumption, automate operations and integrate renewable energy into mining.
                            
Chinese companies are developing solutions that combine automation, digital monitoring, renewable energy and more efficient mineral processing. Such innovations can help African mining operations become more productive and environmentally responsible.
Training African engineers, technicians, geologists, environmental specialists and managers can build local capacity that remains long after individual projects have been completed. Skills transfer turns investment into lasting human capital.
China’s growing experience in green mining and ecological restoration offers another area for practical cooperation. Africa has an opportunity to embrace China’s modern approaches to green mining, water recycling, efficient processing, waste utilisation, land rehabilitation and green energy.
Kenya’s participation in the 2026 China Mining Conference in Tianjin is therefore significant. Mining Cabinet Secretary Hassan Joho used the platform to promote Kenya’s investment opportunities and highlighted deposits of critical minerals including coltan, copper, lithium, niobium and rare earth elements. He also outlined reforms aimed at strengthening governance, transparency and predictability in the sector.
For Kenya, engagement with global mining investors presents an opportunity to attract capital and technology while developing the capabilities needed to participate more meaningfully in the mineral value chain.
China can be an important partner in that journey.
China-Africa cooperation should therefore be viewed not simply through the lens of mineral extraction, but as part of a broader industrial partnership.
Africa has the resources. China has extensive experience in industrialisation, infrastructure development, technology and manufacturing. The combination creates considerable room for cooperation.
If China-Africa mining cooperation continues to focus on value addition, skills transfer, infrastructure, technology, environmental responsibility and local participation, it can help transform Africa’s mineral wealth into a much broader development dividend.
-The writer is a scholar in Nairobi

articles.title: Chivayo, gold and guns: How does Malawi fit in? - Malawi24
articles.summary: Chivayo, gold and guns: How does Malawi fit in?  Malawi24Valentino Phiri walks out  Malawi24
articles.full_text:
Malawi’s former army commander, Paul Valentino Phiri, has been arrested over alleged illegal arms trafficking, with social media commentators linking the case to controversial Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo. The allegations have brought fresh scrutiny to a suspected weapons route into Sudan and the financiers who may have kept it running.
FollowPolitics
The arrest comes amid separate allegations linking Chivayo to Sudanese gold. His access to presidents across the region adds a political dimension to the story, but the available evidence does not establish that he financed the shipments under investigation.
The Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) said retired Valentino Phiri was arrested on Thursday, 1 October, “on five counts relating to abuse of office and dealing in terrorist property”. The bureau said “the charges arise from allegations concerning his role in facilitating illegal arms trafficking in June and July 2025”..
The alleged Malawi route
According to reporting by the Platform for Investigative Journalism (PIJ Malawi), sources alleged that a cargo aircraft carrying heavy weaponry arrived at Kamuzu International Airport, where its cargo was briefly offloaded before being reloaded and flown out.
Documents allegedly identified the Malawi Defence Force as the end-user, while the weapons were reportedly destined for Sudan through Chad. PIJ said it had not seen the alleged intelligence report or the ACB complaint and had not independently established the flight dates, shipping manifests or recipients.
Phiri’s arrest moves the matter into criminal proceedings, but the allegations remain to be proved. The ACB has not publicly identified Chivayo as a financier or participant in the account reviewed for this article.
Chakwera walks in
In August 2021, Chakwera’s office announced that he was expected to travel to South Sudan to witness the arrival of goods exported from Malawi under a trade arrangement. Media reports identified the exports as including maize flour, while subsequent coverage described a deal covering maize, maize flour, groundnuts and beans.
StudyChemistry
That announcement concerned South Sudan, a separate country from Sudan, and preceded the alleged arms trafficking by almost four years. The reporting reviewed provides no evidence connecting those agricultural exports to the case against Phiri. Chivayo’s meeting with then-president Lazarus Chakwera was reported on 15 July 2025, within the period now under investigation. Contemporary reporting also documented his meetings with Kenyan President William Ruto and Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan.
The timing provides a point for investigators to examine, but it does not establish involvement in arms trafficking. Without verified shipment dates, it is also impossible to claim that his Malawi visit occurred days before a weapons flight.
A separate allegation came from Kenyan activist Boniface Mwangi. According to Kenya Insights, Mwangi accused Chivayo in June 2026 of helping Ruto move gold smuggled from Sudan through Dubai.
The publication acknowledged that the accusation was not accompanied by flight manifests, customs records, a financial trail or a named source. The allegation therefore remains unsubstantiated and does not establish a connection to the Malawi shipments.
Kenya’s weapons questions
Kenya’s connection to the Sudan conflict extends beyond allegations about Chivayo. In February 2025, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied groups signed a charter in Nairobi to establish a parallel government.
In June that year, Bellingcat and Kenya’s Daily Nation identified Kenyan-labelled ammunition crates in footage from an alleged RSF depot near Khartoum. Independent weapons specialists examined markings indicating that some ammunition had been intended for Kenya’s Ministry of Defence.
BuyMaps
The investigation did not establish precisely how the crates reached Sudan. Kenya’s Ministry of Defence said it did not recognise the crates or inscriptions and distanced itself from the allegations. Kenya also defended its engagement with the RSF as an effort to promote dialogue and peace.
Those findings present a separate weapons trail requiring answers. They do not establish that the Kenyan-labelled ammunition travelled through Malawi or that Chivayo handled it.
Gold financing the war
The relationship between gold and the RSF’s finances is documented more firmly. In 2023, the United States Treasury identified Al Junaid, a company controlled by RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo and his brother, as a major source of revenue through gold mining and exports.
FollowPolitics
In January 2025, Treasury sanctioned UAE-based Capital Tap Holding, saying it had supplied money and military equipment to the RSF. It also identified AZ Gold as a purchaser of Sudanese gold, presumably for the RSF’s benefit, which subsequently transported the metal to Dubai.
The same announcement described companies used to obscure business dealings and bank accounts accessible to the RSF’s procurement director. These findings document a financing and procurement network supporting the RSF, but do not, by themselves, place Chivayo inside it.
Chivayo’s plane crash
Chivayo died in a helicopter crash on 30 September, a day before Phiri’s arrest. Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa confirmed his death the following day.
Chivayo’s presidential access was unusually public. In August 2026, he shared a video showing Ruto personally ‘chauffer’ driving him and his wife to a waiting helicopter after a family ceremony in Kenya.
TrackExec Orders
He was a prominent supporter of Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa and maintained relationships with Malawi’s political leaders. His meetings with Peter Mutharika were reported in 2019 and again during Mutharika’s current presidency, while his meeting with Chakwera was documented in July 2025.
Those relationships warrant scrutiny where they intersect with public contracts, donations or procurement decisions. Presidential access alone, however, does not establish criminal conduct.
For Malawi, the central questions remain who financed the alleged weapons shipments, who authorised them and whether military end-user documents were used to conceal their destination. Establishing any role for Chivayo will require evidence linking him to the aircraft, cargo, payments or people involved.

articles.title: The New Alamein Agenda: Why Egypt Is India’s Gateway to the African Century - orfonline.org
articles.summary: The New Alamein Agenda: Why Egypt Is India’s Gateway to the African Century  orfonline.org
articles.full_text:
Three continental gatherings on the Egyptian coast offer India a strategic window to deepen its engagement with Africa
Image Source:  Getty Images 
From 2 to 4 October 2026, the Mediterranean coastal city of New Alamein will temporarily transform into the geopolitical and economic capital of the African continent. Egypt is set to host a high-profile trio of continental gatherings: the inaugural Alamein Africa Forum 2026 on investment, the summit of the founding states of the African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD), and the African Union’s eighth mid-year coordination meeting. With heads of state, development financiers, and global business leaders convening on the Egyptian coast, Cairo is sending a clear, unequivocal message about its leadership role in driving African economic integration.
For New Delhi, this convergence of continental leadership should not be viewed merely as a distant diplomatic spectacle. Instead, it is a strategic window of opportunity. As India looks to deepen its footprint in the Global South and secure its economic future amid shifting global supply chains, the momentum generating in New Alamein offers the perfect catalyst to elevate India-Africa cooperation. In this new era, Egypt serves as the indispensable geographic and economic bridge.
In recent years, the relationship between India and Egypt has experienced a renaissance. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s 2023 state visit produced the decision to elevate ties to a strategic partnership covering political, security, defence, economic and scientific cooperation. The bilateral economic fundamentals are undeniably strong. Trade hovered around US$6.5 billion in recent fiscal years, and robust investments from Indian enterprises spanning technology, pharmaceuticals, and manufacturing continue to pour into the Egyptian market. The two governments also expressed the objective of raising bilateral trade to US$12 billion within five years. However, viewing Cairo strictly through the lens of a bilateral partner artificially limits its geopolitical utility. Egypt’s true potential for India lies not just in its domestic market of over 100 million people, but in its unique positioning at the strategic crossroads of Africa, Asia, and Europe.
The traditional model of India-Africa cooperation - historically built on the noble pillars of capacity building, lines of credit, and anti-colonial solidarity - must now evolve into complex, trilateral economic partnerships. Egypt is the ideal catalyst for this transition for three distinct and compelling reasons.

First, Egypt offers unmatched logistical connectivity and an established gateway to the continent's burgeoning markets. A primary challenge for Indian businesses attempting to scale their presence in Africa has been the continent's fragmented infrastructure and complex tariff barriers. Egypt provides a sophisticated workaround. Through the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE) and Egypt's membership in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) - the largest free trade area in the world by the number of participating countries - Indian manufacturers can establish production hubs on Egyptian soil. By manufacturing or assembling in Egypt, Indian firms in sectors like automotives, pharmaceuticals, and agro-processing can access broader African markets with zero or significantly reduced tariffs. This strategic positioning allows Indian businesses to bypass the infrastructural bottlenecks that often hinder direct bilateral trade with sub-Saharan nations, effectively creating a highly resilient supply chain that links Indian innovation to African consumption, while keeping European markets within arm's reach.
Second, the structural priorities of the New Alamein summits currently underway - specifically mobilising resources, advancing regional economic integration, and building resilient partnerships - align seamlessly with India’s core developmental strengths. Africa is currently on the cusp of a massive demographic and digital transition. By 2050, an estimated 1.3 billion people on the continent will be under the age of thirty. India, which has navigated similar developmental imperatives and demographic youth bulges, is uniquely positioned to share its scalable, tested solutions. Trilateral cooperation driven by Indian technology and Egyptian regional influence can dramatically accelerate the deployment of Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) across the continent. India’s success with the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), biometric identity, and accessible telemedicine provides a blueprint for African nations seeking to leapfrog traditional development hurdles. By partnering with Egyptian institutions, which possess a deep understanding of regional regulatory and cultural nuances, Indian tech firms can localise and scale these digital solutions, transforming financial inclusion and healthcare delivery.
Third, both India and Egypt share a critical, existential interest in the green energy transition and the development of sustainable infrastructure. As Africa industrialises, there is a global imperative to ensure this growth does not replicate the carbon-heavy trajectories of the past. Frustrated by the unfulfilled climate finance promises of the developed world, the Global South is increasingly looking inward for solutions. Egypt has proactively positioned itself as a future hub for green hydrogen and renewable-energy-powered industrial clusters, capitalising on its abundant solar and wind resources. India, a leader in the International Solar Alliance with rapidly growing technological expertise in clean energy, is a natural partner in this endeavour. By aligning Indian green capital and engineering prowess with Egypt's strategic location and natural resources, both nations can jointly power African industrialisation. Trilateral ventures in solar grid connectivity, electric vehicle manufacturing, and green hydrogen production can establish a new paradigm for sustainable development.
By explicitly leveraging the India-Egypt Strategic Partnership as a continental launchpad, New Delhi can shift its African engagement into a cohesive, integrated strategy. The road to a robust, future-proof India-Africa partnership runs directly through Cairo.
The three-day diplomatic intensive in New Alamein serves as a potent reminder that Africa is rapidly consolidating its economic architecture and taking charge of its development narrative. The continent is no longer just seeking aid; it is actively seeking equitable partnerships, investment, and technological integration. If India wants to be a foundational partner in the next chapter of the African growth story, it needs reliable, capable, and influential anchor states on the continent. By explicitly leveraging the India-Egypt Strategic Partnership as a continental launchpad, New Delhi can shift its African engagement into a cohesive, integrated strategy. The road to a robust, future-proof India-Africa partnership runs directly through Cairo. It is time for Indian policymakers to recognise Egypt not just as a lucrative destination, but as the primary catalyst for a shared, prosperous future.

articles.title: German defence giant plans South African production line for drone bomb with 15 km range - africa.businessinsider.com
articles.summary: German defence giant plans South African production line for drone bomb with 15 km range  africa.businessinsider.com
articles.full_text:
- Rheinmetall Denel Munition plans to start a LongClaw production line in the second half of 2027.
- The company says the South African designed glide bomb has a range of about 15 km when released from roughly 4.9 km.
- It is aimed mainly at military drones, although the company says it can also be launched from crewed aircraft.
- Small quantities are being assembled manually; no South African military order or export contract was announced.
Rheinmetall Denel Munition, known as RDM, expects to start a production line for its LongClaw glide bomb in the second half of 2027, according to its chief executive, Maximilian Froch.
The weapon weighs 7.5 kilograms and carries a 3-kilogram warhead. RDM says it can travel about 15 kilometres when released from an altitude of roughly 4.9 kilometres. That range describes a particular release condition- it is not a fixed distance the bomb would travel from every altitude.
DON'T MISS THIS: From selling its tech to Ukraine to partnering with an Indian billionaire, South African aerospace firm unveils its new drone
LongClaw is designed chiefly for unmanned aircraft. Unlike a drone that flies into its target, it is a separate weapon released by an aircraft. Its wings allow it to glide towards a target, while a satellite-based system guides it.
RDM says small quantities are already being assembled manually and that the weapon has undergone evaluation on several drone platforms. The company has not announced that a full production line is operating, nor has it identified a confirmed buyer.
He said LongClaw was designed entirely in South Africa and that most of its components would be made locally. “We have tried to have the most indigenous solution possible,” he said.
A South African design in a German group’s portfolio
RDM is a South African company jointly owned by Rheinmetall’s German ammunition business, which holds 51%, and South African state defence company Denel, which holds the remainder.
DON'T MISS THIS:South Africa makes record arms sales of over $550 million to France, Turkey, Kenya, UAE and 38 others
It already produces other types of ammunition and markets products internationally. Rheinmetall identified LongClaw as a drone-deployable glide bomb when presenting its defence products in June.
That makes the production plan significant for South Africa’s defence industry. A locally designed weapon could be manufactured through a company with established international sales channels, though that does not guarantee export orders.
RDM says it is also trying to interest the South African National Defence Force in LongClaw. Froch told DefenceWeb that international sales would require approval from South Africa’s arms export authorities. Neither domestic procurement nor an overseas sale was announced.
Mock-ups of the bomb were displayed on two South African aircraft designs at September’s Africa Aerospace and Defence exhibition, Paramount’s V-Raven drone and its Mwari aircraft. A display showing how a weapon could be carried should not be mistaken for confirmation that either aircraft has entered service with LongClaw.
For now, LongClaw’s confirmed position is narrower than a completed military upgrade: it is a South African designed weapon undergoing development and evaluation, with a production line planned for next year.

articles.title: Trump administration shifts funds from human rights to supporting far-right causes - CNN
articles.summary: Trump administration shifts funds from human rights to supporting far-right causes  CNNTrump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad | US foreign policy  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
The US State Department directed millions of dollars originally earmarked to promote human rights to promote far-right causes including Afrikaner rights in South Africa, safeguarding “Western civilizational norms,” and documenting “backsliding” in Europe related to mass migration, a source familiar with the matter told CNN.
The funds, which come from the nearly $177 million in Democracy Funds, were obligated despite concerns and holds by the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, the source said. They were due to lapse on Wednesday, the last day of the fiscal year.
The proposed causes align with the Trump administration’s broader shifts away from traditional human rights to focus on causes like alleged free-speech suppression and mass migration in Europe as well as “natural rights.” Two of the proposed grants are focused on Brazil and South Africa – countries where the administration has clashed with the governments – and a third is focused on Nigeria, where the administration has alleged “mass slaughter” of Christians.
It marks another instance of the administration bypassing Congress on funding matters, following its move to cancel $810 million of funding that has been appropriated by Congress for refugees, immigrants and other services.
Typically, the money from the Democracy Funds is used to support programs in authoritarian countries or those with limited democracies, the source said. Instead, the proposed grants, which were first reported by The Guardian, include funding for programs in Europe and the United Kingdom.
Asked about the funds, an unnamed State Department spokesperson said they had completed congressional notification requirements.
“The President promised to combat the destructive woke agenda that has done so much damage to our country and to the world,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said. “We will never apologize for defending Western civilization, opposing censorship, ending the era of mass migration, and taking action against government-sponsored race-based discrimination in South Africa.”
According to the source familiar with the matter, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had signed off on a memo to obligate the funds despite the ongoing holds. Senate Foreign Relations Committee ranking member Sen. Jeanne Shaheen had put holds on 10 proposed awards worth a total of $22 million.
The grants have buy-in from the highest levels of the White House, including Vice President JD Vance, the source said. The White House referred to the State Department for comment.
“Congress appropriated money for the Democracy Fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” Shaheen in a statement.
“In bypassing Congress, the Trump Administration is now using taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies,” the New Hampshire Democrat said. “This is a waste of resources and undermines American values and our relationships with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”
The proposed grants that had holds include one to combat alleged judicial overreach and censorship in Brazil. The Trump administration has clashed with the Lula government and had imposed sanctions on Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the trial of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally. The sanctions were lifted in December. However, the US has also revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US and President Donald Trump has met with Flávio Bolsonaro, Jair Bolsonaro’s son who is running for president in Brazil.
Other proposed grants focus on Europe, including a $5 million award to support the development of “a civilizational alliance in Europe through research, public debates, and policy reform to safeguard freedom of expression, political competition, and national sovereignty.”
Top administration officials, including Vance, have lambasted European nations over allegations of free speech backsliding while also meeting with far-right European political figures.
Samuel Samson, a top appointee in the State Department’s Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor, argued last year for the need for “civilizational allies” in Europe.
“Our hope is that both Europe and the United States can recommit to our Western heritage, and that European nations will end the weaponization of government against those seeking to defend it,” he wrote.
The Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor has undergone significant changes under the second Trump administration.
As CNN reported last year, the US State Department will require its diplomats describe enforcement of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies, alleged facilitation of mass migration, and government funding that supports abortion medications as “human rights infringements” in its next human rights report. The report will also shift focus to “natural rights” like freedom of speech, an official said at the time, in a move likely to target traditional European allies for alleged freedom of speech restrictions.
